details:
**Sethe kills her daughter**
The central event of Toni Morrison's 1987 novel Beloved. When the slave catcher Schoolteacher arrives to take her family back into slavery, the escaped slave Sethe runs into the woodshed and cuts her infant daughter's throat to keep her from being enslaved. The episode is based on the real case of Margaret Garner.

**124 Bluestone Road**
The house outside Cincinnati, Ohio, where most of the novel takes place. The novel opens by calling it "spiteful," "full of a baby's venom," because the ghost of Sethe's murdered daughter haunts it. Sethe lives there with her daughter Denver.

**Beloved (the title character)**
A mysterious young woman who walks out of a stream fully dressed and appears in front of 124 just after Sethe, Paul D, and Denver return from a carnival. She has the name carved on the dead baby's headstone and seems to be the dead daughter returned in flesh. She drives Paul D out of the house and consumes Sethe's life until the community's women drive her away.

**Paul D and the "tobacco tin" heart**
A fellow former slave from Sweet Home who arrives at 124 years later and becomes Sethe's lover. He has locked his painful memories in the "tobacco tin" of his heart, whose lid rusts shut and then breaks open. He tells Sethe her love is "too thick."

**Schoolteacher**
The cruel, pseudo-scientific overseer who takes over the Sweet Home plantation after Mr. Garner's death. He has his nephews record the slaves' "animal characteristics" and steal Sethe's breast milk. When she recognizes his hat years later, she hears hummingbird wings and thinks "No. No. Nono" before fleeing to the woodshed.

**Sethe attacks Mr. Bodwin with an ice pick**
In the climax, the white abolitionist Mr. Bodwin drives up to 124 to collect Denver, who is going to work for his household. Sethe mistakes him for Schoolteacher returning and attacks him with an ice pick. The women of the community restrain her, and Beloved disappears.

**The chokecherry tree scars**
The mass of scars on Sethe's back from a whipping at Sweet Home. Amy Denver, a runaway white girl who helps Sethe give birth to Denver during her escape, describes them as a blossoming chokecherry tree, and Paul D later kisses the "tree."

**Sweet Home**
The Kentucky plantation where Sethe, Paul D, Halle, Sixo, and others were enslaved under the relatively mild Mr. Garner and then under Schoolteacher. Most of the novel's flashbacks to slavery take place there.

**Baby Suggs and the Clearing**
Sethe's mother-in-law, an "unchurched preacher" who led gatherings in the Clearing, where she urged former slaves to love their own flesh. After the infanticide she gives up and takes to her bed, where she thinks only about "harmless" colors like blue and yellow, staring at two orange squares on a quilt until she dies.

**Stamp Paid**
A former slave who ferries Sethe and the newborn Denver across the Ohio River to freedom. He later shows Paul D a newspaper clipping about the infanticide and visits 124 often.

**Denver**
Sethe's surviving daughter, named after Amy Denver and born during the escape. She is jealous of Paul D and possessive of Beloved, and she eventually leaves the yard to seek help from the community and work for the Bodwins. At the Bodwins' house there is a racist figurine of a Black boy with coins in his mouth and the words "At Yo' Service" on its base.

**Howard and Buglar**
Sethe's two sons, who run away from 124 because of the ghost's haunting. They leave after a mirror shatters and tiny handprints appear in a cake.

**Halle and the butter**
Sethe's husband, Baby Suggs's son. He secretly watched Schoolteacher's nephews steal Sethe's milk and went mad. Paul D last saw him sitting by the churn with butter smeared all over his face.

**Paul D's iron bit and the chain gang**
Paul D was once forced to wear an iron bit in his mouth while the rooster Mister watched him, a humiliation he never forgets. Later he escapes a chain gang in Georgia and follows the flowering blossoms north to freedom.

**Sixo and the Thirty-Mile Woman**
A Sweet Home slave who walks thirty miles to visit his lover, the "Thirty-Mile Woman." Schoolteacher's men catch him and burn him alive. As he dies he laughs and shouts "Seven-O!", celebrating the child she is carrying.

**The engraved headstone and "You your best thing"**
Sethe had sex with an engraver in exchange for carving the single word "Beloved" on her daughter's headstone. Near the end, Paul D tells Sethe "You your best thing, Sethe. You are," and that line later titled Tarana Burke and Brené Brown's anthology You Are Your Best Thing.
